title: Measuring Health and Fitness
description: Standard fitness tests for each component of health and fitness, their protocols, and comparison against normative data.
content_html:
Why Do We Test Fitness?

Fitness testing is used to measure the components of health and fitness in a structured, repeatable way. Before a coach or sport scientist can design a training programme, they need objective data — numbers that show exactly where an athlete's strengths and weaknesses lie. Testing also provides a baseline measurement that future test scores can be compared against. Crucially, fitness tests only give meaningful information when they are both valid and reliable. A test that varies due to warm-up differences, time of day or examiner technique cannot be fairly compared to previous results or to normative data tables.

Aerobic Endurance Tests

Two tests measure cardiovascular endurance. The multistage fitness test (also called the bleep test or 20-metre shuttle run) requires the participant to run between two lines 20 metres apart, keeping pace with an audio recording that plays beeps at increasing intervals. The speed increases each minute (each level) and the test ends when the participant can no longer reach the line in time or voluntarily drops out. The level and shuttle number at which the participant stops is recorded and compared to normative data tables to give a rating from very poor to excellent. The test is progressive and maximal, making it highly specific to aerobic endurance.

The Cooper 12-minute run offers an alternative. The participant runs as far as possible in exactly 12 minutes on a measured track. The total distance covered (in metres) is recorded and matched against normative data by age and gender. A well-conditioned male aged 15–16 might cover over 2,800 metres; a score below 2,100 metres would be rated poor. The test is simple to administer and requires only a stopwatch and a measured surface.

Key Fact

Two tests measure aerobic (cardiovascular) endurance: the multistage fitness test (20-metre shuttle run with progressive beeps, record the level/shuttle reached) and the Cooper 12-minute run (record total distance covered). Both use normative data tables to rate the result.

Flexibility, Muscular Endurance and Strength Tests

The sit-and-reach test measures flexibility of the lower back and hamstrings. The participant sits on the floor with legs straight and feet flat against a sit-and-reach box. They reach forward with both hands as far as possible along the measuring scale and hold the position for two seconds. The furthest point reached (in centimetres) is recorded — positive values are beyond the feet, negative values fall short. Three attempts are usually made and the best score used. Results are compared to normative data tables by age and gender.

Muscular endurance is measured with either the one-minute press-up test or the one-minute sit-up test. For press-ups, the participant begins in the standard press-up position (or box position for females in some versions) and performs as many full-range press-ups as possible in 60 seconds — chest to the floor and arms fully extended on each repetition. For sit-ups, the participant lies on their back with knees bent at 90 degrees and hands placed on thighs; they curl up until the hands reach the knees, then lower back down. The number of complete repetitions in 60 seconds is recorded and compared to normative data.

Muscular strength is tested either using a grip dynamometer or a one-repetition maximum (one-rep max). In the grip dynamometer test, the participant holds the device at their side and squeezes as hard as possible for a few seconds; three attempts are taken (alternating hands) and the best score (in kilograms) is recorded. The one-rep max test requires the participant to lift the heaviest single repetition possible for a given exercise (e.g. bench press or squat); this is found by working up in weight until only one full repetition can be completed with correct technique. Results are compared to normative data relative to the participant's body weight.

Speed, Power, Agility, Balance and Reaction Time Tests

The 30-metre sprint test measures speed. The participant starts from a standing position and sprints flat-out over 30 metres; time is recorded using either manual stopwatches or electronic timing gates. Three trials are usually taken and the best time used. Results are compared to normative data tables by age and gender — an elite youth sprinter might record under 4.0 seconds.

Power (explosive strength) is most commonly assessed using the vertical jump test (also called the Sargent jump). The participant stands next to a wall, reaches as high as possible with one hand and marks the reach height (chalk or measuring tape). They then jump as high as possible from a standing position and mark the peak jump height. The difference between the two heights (in centimetres) gives the jump height, which is recorded and compared to normative data. The standing broad jump is an alternative power test where the participant jumps horizontally from a standing position and the distance from the take-off line to the nearest landing point is measured.

The Illinois agility run measures agility — the ability to change direction quickly and accurately while moving at speed. The participant lies face down at the start line. On the signal, they sprint to the far end of the course, weave around a series of cones placed in a set pattern, and sprint back to the finish. The time taken (in seconds) is recorded. A typical course is 10 metres long and 5 metres wide; the total run with the cone weave covers approximately 60 metres of movement. Results are compared to normative data by age and gender.

Balance is measured using the stork stand test. The participant stands on their dominant foot with the other foot resting flat against the inside of the supporting knee, hands placed on the hips. On the signal they raise their heel and balance on the ball of the foot; the timer starts when the heel lifts and stops when balance is lost (heel touches ground, non-supporting foot moves, or hands leave hips). Three attempts are made and the best time (in seconds) is recorded and compared to normative data.

Key Fact

Speed = 30-metre sprint (record best time). Power = vertical/Sargent jump (difference between standing reach and jump height). Agility = Illinois agility run (weave cones, record time; start lying down). Balance = stork stand (balance on ball of dominant foot, record time). Reaction time = ruler drop test (record distance converted to milliseconds).

Reaction time is tested with the ruler drop test. The tester holds a ruler vertically at the 0 cm mark between the participant's open thumb and forefinger at the 0 cm level without touching it. Without warning, the tester drops the ruler and the participant catches it as quickly as possible. The distance the ruler fell (in centimetres) is recorded; this is converted to reaction time in milliseconds using a standard conversion table (for example, a drop of 15 cm corresponds to approximately 175 milliseconds). Five trials are taken and the average used. The test is simple but has limited reliability if the tester gives visual cues before releasing.

Normative Data and Why It Matters

Normative data allows a raw test result to be given context. A grip strength reading of 40 kg means little on its own, but compared to a normative table it might be rated as above average for a 16-year-old male. Normative data also allows coaches to set realistic goals and to monitor progress over time. However, comparisons are only valid when testing conditions are standardised — the same warm-up, equipment, time of day and examiner technique must be used each time. Any change in conditions threatens the reliability and therefore the validity of the comparison.

A test is valid if it actually measures the component it claims to measure. For example, the sit-and-reach test is a valid measure of lower-back and hamstring flexibility — but it is not a valid measure of shoulder flexibility. A test is reliable if repeated testing under the same conditions produces the same result. Reliability can be threatened by factors such as varying warm-up duration, different equipment calibration, inconsistent instructions from the tester, or the participant's physical state on the day. If a test is reliable but not valid, it is measuring the wrong thing consistently. If it is valid but not reliable, results will fluctuate for reasons unrelated to actual fitness changes. Both properties are required before test data can be meaningfully compared with normative tables or previous personal scores.

The one-rep max test is arguably the hardest to standardise safely because the participant must work to their absolute maximum, increasing injury risk, and "full range of motion" can be interpreted differently by different testers. The ruler drop test is susceptible to anticipation — if the tester gives a visual cue (e.g. a slight finger movement before releasing), the participant may react to the cue rather than the drop, giving a falsely fast score. The stork stand can be affected by the surface — a soft mat versus a hard floor changes the difficulty significantly. In an exam, showing awareness that each test has potential threats to reliability will earn higher marks on evaluate questions.
exam_tip_html: Protocol questions are common in the written examination — they typically ask you to "describe" a fitness test for 2 or 3 marks. Structure your answer as: (1) what the participant does, (2) what is measured or recorded, and (3) how results are compared (normative data). Avoid vague language like "they run a lot" — use precise terms such as "20 metres", "on the signal", "best of three attempts". For reliability/validity questions, always state both terms and define the difference: validity = measures what it claims to; reliability = produces consistent results under the same conditions. Confusing the two is a common error that loses marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Each component of health and fitness has at least one standard test: bleep test or Cooper run (aerobic endurance), sit-and-reach (flexibility), one-minute press-up/sit-up (muscular endurance), grip dynamometer or one-rep max (strength), 30-metre sprint (speed), vertical/Sargent jump (power), Illinois agility run (agility), stork stand (balance), ruler drop test (reaction time).
  • Test results are compared against normative data tables (by age and gender) to give a meaningful rating and to set targets for improvement.
  • For comparisons to be valid, tests must be both reliable (consistent conditions) and valid (measuring the correct component) — any change in protocol threatens the accuracy of comparisons with past scores or normative data.

practice_questions.text:
Which fitness test is used to measure agility?
A) Stork stand
B) Ruler drop test
C) Illinois agility run
D) Vertical jump test

State the fitness test used to measure each of the following components:
(a) Aerobic endurance
(b) Balance
practice_questions.marks: (a) One mark for either: multistage fitness test (bleep test / 20-metre shuttle run) OR Cooper 12-minute run. (b) One mark for: stork stand (stork balance test). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the protocol for the ruler drop test, used to measure reaction time.
practice_questions.marks: One mark per valid protocol point up to 3 marks from: tester holds ruler vertically at 0 cm between participant's open thumb and forefinger (1) / tester drops ruler without warning and participant catches it as quickly as possible (1) / the distance the ruler falls is recorded in centimetres and converted to milliseconds using a conversion table (1) / several trials are taken and the average used (1). Maximum 3 marks. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between the validity and reliability of a fitness test.
practice_questions.marks: Validity (up to 2 marks): a test is valid if it actually measures the component it claims to measure, e.g. the sit-and-reach is a valid measure of lower-back and hamstring flexibility (2 marks for definition + example; 1 mark for definition alone). Reliability (up to 2 marks): a test is reliable if repeated testing under the same conditions produces consistent results, e.g. if warm-up, equipment and instructions change between tests the results cannot be reliably compared (2 marks for definition + consequence; 1 mark for definition alone). [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A sports coach wants to test the muscular strength and aerobic endurance of a group of 16-year-old athletes before designing their training programme.

Describe an appropriate fitness test for each component and explain how the results could be used.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two tests described with clear protocol detail and clear explanation of use. Strength: grip dynamometer test — participant squeezes as hard as possible, best of three attempts recorded in kilograms, compared to normative data to rate the athlete's strength relative to their age group; result provides a baseline and identifies whether strength training is a priority. Aerobic endurance: multistage fitness test — participant runs 20-metre shuttles in time with progressive beeps, level and shuttle reached recorded and compared to normative data; result highlights cardiovascular fitness and informs target training zones. Both tests must be reliable (same conditions each time) and valid to allow meaningful comparison with normative data.
Secure (3-4 marks): Both tests named with some protocol detail and some explanation of use.
Developing (2 marks): One test described adequately or both named without protocol detail.
Emerging (1 mark): One test named only. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A female 400-metre runner scores 14.3 seconds on the Illinois agility run and 38 cm on the vertical jump test. Her coach notes that both scores fall in the 'below average' band for her age group according to normative data tables.

Evaluate how useful normative data is for measuring and improving this athlete's fitness.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Balanced evaluation of the usefulness of normative data with specific reference to the scenario. Arguments for usefulness: scores below average for agility and power give the coach objective targets; normative data provides a standardised benchmark allowing comparison across athletes; helps prioritise which components to train first. Arguments against or limitations: normative data may not reflect the specific demands of 400-metre running — agility may not be a priority component; general population tables may not be appropriate for elite-level comparisons (athlete-specific normative data is better); if testing conditions were not fully standardised the comparison is unreliable; normative data shows where the athlete stands but does not explain why or how to improve. Substantiated judgement: normative data is a useful starting point for identifying areas below the expected range, but its value depends entirely on the validity and reliability of the test — coaches should use it alongside sport-specific performance data rather than in isolation.
Secure (5-6 marks): Clear points on both sides with some application to the scenario and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Mainly one-sided with limited reference to scenario.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points about normative data with no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which fitness test measures aerobic endurance by recording the level and shuttle number at which the participant can no longer keep pace with the audio beeps?
In the stork stand test, timing begins when the participant raises their heel and stops when balance is lost. What component of fitness does this test measure?
In the sit-and-reach test, the participant sits with legs straight and feet against the box, then reaches forward as far as possible. The score is the furthest point reached in _____.
A fitness test is _____ if it produces consistent results each time it is administered under the same conditions, making comparisons with normative data meaningful.
Match each fitness test to the component it measures.
right: Muscular strength — heaviest single lift completed with correct technique
Agility — time taken to sprint and weave around a set cone course
Reaction time — distance ruler falls before participant catches it, converted to milliseconds

flashcard_questions.q: What two tests can be used to measure aerobic endurance?
flashcard_questions.a: Multistage fitness test (bleep test) and the Cooper 12-minute run.

flashcard_questions.q: In the multistage fitness test, what does the participant do and what is recorded?
flashcard_questions.a: Runs 20m shuttles to beeps; level and shuttle reached are recorded.

flashcard_questions.q: In the Cooper 12-minute run, what is measured?
flashcard_questions.a: The total distance covered in metres within exactly 12 minutes.

flashcard_questions.q: Describe the protocol for the sit-and-reach flexibility test in one sentence.
flashcard_questions.a: Sit legs straight, reach forward as far as possible; record the distance.

flashcard_questions.q: Which two tests measure muscular endurance?
flashcard_questions.a: The one-minute press-up test and the one-minute sit-up test.

flashcard_questions.q: Which two tests measure muscular strength?
flashcard_questions.a: The grip dynamometer test and the one-repetition maximum (one-rep max) test.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the vertical (Sargent) jump test measure, and how is the score calculated?
flashcard_questions.a: Power; the difference between standing reach height and jump height.

flashcard_questions.q: Describe the starting position for the Illinois agility run.
flashcard_questions.a: Lying face down at the start line, then sprints on the signal.

flashcard_questions.q: What component does the stork stand test measure, and when does timing stop?
flashcard_questions.a: Balance; stops when heel touches the floor or hands leave the hips.

flashcard_questions.q: In the ruler drop test, what is measured and how is it converted to reaction time?
flashcard_questions.a: Distance fallen in centimetres, converted to milliseconds via a conversion table.

flashcard_questions.q: What is normative data, and why is it used in fitness testing?
flashcard_questions.a: Age/gender score tables used to rate a result and set improvement targets.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between a valid and a reliable fitness test?
flashcard_questions.a: Valid measures the right component; reliable gives consistent results each time.

glossary_terms.definition: An initial measurement taken before a training programme begins, used as a reference point for comparing future results.
A valid test measures the specific component it claims to measure, with no significant influence from other factors.
A reliable test produces consistent results each time it is administered under the same conditions.
Normative data tables show the expected range of scores for a given test, broken down by age and gender, allowing an individual result to be rated against a comparable population.
A progressive, shuttle-run test in which participants run 20 metres back and forth in time with beeps that increase in pace each level; also called the bleep test.
